questions.question: A sign at the Vancouver aquarium says 6 348 people visited on Saturday. What is the value of the digit 3 in 6 348?
questions.explain: Read the places from the right: 8 ones, 4 tens, 3 hundreds, 6 thousands, so the 3 is worth 3 × 100 = 300. The common trap is naming the digit by itself (3) or slipping one place over and saying 30.

questions.question: Aria colours 7 of the 100 equal squares on a hundred grid. Which decimal shows the coloured part of the grid?
questions.explain: The whole grid is 1, so each small square is one hundredth, and 7 squares is seven hundredths = 0.07. The common trap is writing 0.7, which is 7 tenths — that would be 70 squares.

questions.question: Rowan's class marks fractions in sixths on a number line. Which fraction is closest to 1 whole?
questions.explain: When the denominators are the same, the fraction with the bigger numerator is bigger, and 5/6 needs only one more sixth to reach 8/8... to reach 6/6, one whole. The common trap is choosing 3/6, which sits exactly at the one-half benchmark, not near 1.

questions.question: Milo buys a day pass for the SeaBus for $6.75 and pays with a $20 bill. How much change should he get?
questions.explain: Count up from $6.75: 25¢ brings you to $7.00, then $13 more brings you to $20.00, so the change is $13.25. The common trap is subtracting the dollars first and forgetting to regroup one dollar into 100 cents, which gives $14.25.

questions.question: Four schools collected bottles for a fundraiser: Maple 4 807, Cedar 4 078, Birch 4 780, Alder 4 087. Which number of bottles is the SECOND greatest?
questions.explain: Compare place by place from the left: all have 4 thousands, so look at hundreds — 8, 7, 0, 0 — making 4 807 the greatest and 4 780 the second greatest. The common trap is answering with the greatest number, or judging by the last digit instead of the biggest place.

questions.question: Owen measures the rain gauge at school: 1.6 cm on Monday and 0.85 cm on Tuesday. How much rain fell in the two days altogether?
questions.explain: Line up the decimal points and think of 1.6 as 1.60: 0 + 5 = 5 hundredths, 6 + 8 = 14 tenths, which regroups to 1 one and 4 tenths, giving 2.45 cm. The common traps are lining up the right-hand ends instead of the decimal points (1.91) or forgetting to regroup the 14 tenths (1.45).

questions.question: Leo's family cuts a pan of blueberry bars into 8 equal pieces. Leo eats 2/8 of the pan and his sister eats 3/8 of the pan. What fraction of the pan is LEFT?
questions.explain: The pieces are all eighths, so add only the numerators: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8 eaten, then 8/8 − 5/8 = 3/8 left. The common traps are adding the denominators straight across to get 5/16, or stopping at 5/8, which is the part eaten, not the part left.

questions.question: Hana has $20.00 at the Saturday farmers market. She buys 2 baskets of blueberries at $4.50 each and a loaf of bread for $5.25. She then sees a bouquet of flowers for $6.00. Can she buy it?
options: Yes — she has $10.25 left, so she can buy the bouquet.
No — she has $5.75 left, so she is 25¢ short.
Yes — she has $6.75 left, so she can buy the bouquet.
Yes — she has $5.75 left, so she can buy the bouquet.
questions.explain: Two baskets cost 2 × $4.50 = $9.00, and $9.00 + $5.25 = $14.25 spent, so $20.00 − $14.25 = $5.75 left — 25¢ less than the $6.00 bouquet. The common traps are paying for only one basket, or forgetting to regroup a dollar into 100 cents while subtracting, which gives $6.75.
